about.p2: With a focus on user experience and performance, I strive to build products that make a difference.

whatIsThis.title: What is this?
whatIsThis.p1: My QOL Scripts (MQS) is a client-side scripting mod that brings the power of modern JavaScript to Minecraft. Think of it as a programmable extension layer that lets you customize your gameplay experience through scripts you can write, share, and manage entirely within the game.
whatIsThis.p2: Unlike traditional mods that require recompilation and JAR packaging, MQS scripts are simple JavaScript files that you can write in any text editor and drop into a folder. The mod discovers, loads, and manages these scripts dynamically, giving you immediate feedback without restarting the game.

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.intro: MQS is architected around a modular system where each script is treated as a first-class module with an explicit lifecycle. The project is built entirely in Java 21 and leverages several advanced technologies to create a seamless scripting experience:
overview.architectureAlt: Architecture diagram showing the main components and their interactions

coreArchitecture.title: Core Architecture
coreArchitecture.intro: The mod is organized into focused packages under net.me.*, each handling a specific aspect of the scripting platform:
coreArchitecture.scriptingEngine: **Scripting Engine** (net.me.scripting): The heart of MQS, powered by GraalVM's GraalJS engine. It includes the ScriptDiscoverer that scans the scripts directory for @module(...) declarations, a ScriptContextManager that pools Graal contexts for optimal performance, and lifecycle management for enabling/disabling scripts.
coreArchitecture.eventSystem: **Event System** (net.me.event): A custom event bus layered on top of Fabric hooks. The EventManager tracks per-phase listeners and bridges Fabric events through FabricEventAdapter, ensuring that events are properly isolated per RunningScript.
coreArchitecture.runtimeHooking: **Runtime Hooking** (net.me.hooking): Powered by ByteBuddy, this system enables in-memory method interception at runtime. The HookManager installs a Java agent, resolves Yarn mappings to stable class names, and applies or removes hooks dynamically based on script requests.
coreArchitecture.userInterfaces: **User Interfaces** (net.me.ui): A complete in-game GUI built on top of Minecraft's native rendering system, including a scripts menu, console, keybinds configuration, and settings screens.
coreArchitecture.commandSystem: **Command System** (net.me.command): Registers custom client-side commands with the /mqs command tree, featuring argument parsing and tab-completion.
coreArchitecture.keybindManagement: **Keybind Management** (net.me.keybinds): Allows scripts to register custom keybinds that can be reconfigured in-game, with full integration into Minecraft's keybind system.
coreArchitecture.configuration: **Configuration** (net.me.config): A persistent configuration system that stores both global mod settings (mqs_config.json) and per-script configurations, with automatic saving and loading.

techStack.title: Technology Stack
techStack.graalvm: **GraalVM JavaScript**: ES2024-compliant JavaScript engine with high-performance JIT compilation
techStack.bytebuddy: **ByteBuddy**: Runtime code generation for method hooking and Java class extension
techStack.fabric: **Fabric API**: Minecraft modding framework providing game integration
techStack.yarn: **Yarn Mappings**: Stable, human-readable class and method names for Minecraft
techStack.lombok: **Lombok**: Reduces boilerplate code in Java classes

discovery.title: Script Discovery and Loading
discovery.intro: MQS uses a custom annotation-based discovery system. Scripts declare themselves with an @module annotation:
discovery.explanation: The ScriptDiscoverer scans the myqolscripts/scripts directory, parses these annotations, and creates ScriptDescriptor objects that store metadata. When a script is enabled, a RunningScript instance is created with its own Graal context, isolating it from other scripts.

javaInterop.title: Java Interoperability
javaInterop.intro: One of MQS's most powerful features is its deep Java integration. Scripts can import Java classes, call methods, and even extend Minecraft classes using the stable Yarn mappings:
javaInterop.extend: For advanced use cases, scripts can extend Java classes:

hooking.title: Runtime Method Hooking
hooking.intro: The hooking system is built on ByteBuddy and allows scripts to intercept Java method calls at runtime. Hooks can be installed before or after method execution, with access to method arguments, return values, and the calling context:
hooking.useCase: This enables powerful use cases like the included FullBright script, which hooks into Minecraft's gamma validation to bypass brightness limits.

performance.title: Performance Considerations
performance.intro: Performance is a core design principle in MQS:
performance.contextPooling: **Context Pooling**: Graal contexts are expensive to create, so ScriptContextManager maintains a pool that's recycled when scripts are disabled.
performance.selectiveRetransformation: **Selective Retransformation**: ByteBuddy retransformation only occurs when hooks are actually installed, minimizing overhead.
performance.threadSafety: **Thread Safety**: All Minecraft-facing work is scheduled onto the client thread through McUtils to prevent race conditions.
performance.lazyLoading: **Lazy Class Loading**: Java classes accessed from scripts are loaded lazily via LazyJsClassHolder to reduce initialization time.

security.title: Security
security.intro: MQS implements a conservative security model by default:
security.classWhitelisting: **Class Whitelisting**: ScriptingClassResolver restricts class access to whitelisted packages unless GlobalConfigManager.allowAllClasses is explicitly enabled.
security.isolatedContexts: **Isolated Contexts**: Each script runs in its own Graal context, preventing scripts from interfering with each other.
security.controlledHooks: **Controlled Hooks**: Hooks are automatically removed when scripts are disabled, ensuring clean state restoration.

installation.title: Installation
installation.step2: Download Fabric API and My QOL Scripts from GitHub
installation.step3: Place both .jar files in your .minecraft/mods folder
installation.jvmArgs: For optimal performance, add these JVM arguments to enable GraalJS's high-speed JIT compiler:

firstScript.title: Creating Your First Script
firstScript.intro: Scripts go in .minecraft/myqolscripts/scripts/. Here's a simple example that sends a chat message when enabled:

inGame.title: In-Game Management
inGame.intro: MQS provides a comprehensive in-game interface for managing scripts:
inGame.scriptsMenu: **Scripts Menu** (default: F10): View all available scripts, enable/disable them, and access their configuration
inGame.console: **Integrated Console**: Execute commands, view script output, and debug issues
inGame.keybinds: **Keybinds Screen**: View and rebind keybinds registered by scripts
inGame.settings: **Settings Screen**: Configure global mod options like class access and log redirection
inGame.consoleCommands: The integrated console supports commands like:
inGame.cmdList: list - Show all discovered scripts and their status

opinion.title: Personal Opinion
opinion.intro: Building MQS has been an incredible journey that pushed my understanding of several complex domains:
opinion.consoleAlt: Screenshot showing the in-game console with output from running scripts
opinion.graalChallenge: The biggest challenge was integrating a JavaScript engine into a Java application while maintaining performance and security. GraalVM's polyglot API made this possible, but learning to properly manage contexts, handle interop, and avoid memory leaks required deep understanding of both GraalJS and the JVM.
opinion.hookingChallenge: The hooking system powered by ByteBuddy was another significant challenge. Java's built-in instrumentation API is powerful, but using it safely in a game environment where code needs to be hot-swapped and hooks must be cleanly removed is non-trivial. I spent considerable time ensuring that hooks are properly disposed and that the game remains stable even when scripts are poorly written.
opinion.architecture: I'm particularly proud of the architecture's modularity. Each manager has a clear responsibility, and the facade pattern in ScriptingService provides a clean API for the UI and command systems without exposing implementation details. This separation makes the codebase maintainable and testable.
opinion.lifecycle: The decision to use explicit lifecycles for scripts (enable/disable methods) rather than simple "load on startup" was deliberate. This gives scripts control over their initialization and cleanup, preventing resource leaks and allowing for better error handling.
opinion.future: Looking forward, I'd like to improve the documentation, add more examples, and potentially create a marketplace where users can share scripts. The full potential of MQS is in its community, and I hope to see players creating innovative scripts that enhance everyone's Minecraft experience.
opinion.cta: If you're interested in trying MQS or contributing, check out the GitHub repository. The mod is licensed under AGPLv3, and I'm happy to discuss alternative licensing for open-source projects that would benefit from the codebase.

whatIsThis.title: What is this?
whatIsThis.p1: Mend is a command-line tool designed to reliably apply diffs, especially those generated by Large Language Models (LLMs). Where standard patch tools fail due to incorrect line numbers or slightly-off context, Mend excels.
whatIsThis.p2: It ignores line numbers and uses a powerful fuzzy-matching engine combined with an interactive conflict resolution system to ensure your changes land exactly where they should. Think of it as a smarter, more forgiving patch utility built for the AI age.

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.intro: Mend is built entirely in Rust for performance and reliability. It parses diff files, intelligently matches hunks to their target locations using multiple strategies, and applies changes safely with user confirmation when needed.

features.title: Key Features
features.interactive: **Interactive Conflict Resolution**: Never get stuck on a failed patch again. If Mend can't find a perfect spot or finds multiple possibilities, it prompts you to choose the correct location, skip the hunk, or abort safely.
features.ciMode: **CI/Scripting Friendly**: Use the --ci flag to run in non-interactive mode. It fails with a non-zero exit code on any ambiguity, perfect for automated workflows.
features.clipboard: **Clipboard & Stdin Support**: Paste a diff directly from your clipboard with -c or pipe it from tools like git diff.
features.fuzzyMatching: **Powerful Fuzzy Matching**: A multi-stage algorithm finds the correct patch location even with formatting changes, modified context lines, or LLM-induced noise.
features.gitDiff: **Full Git Diff Support**: Seamlessly handles file creations, deletions, and modifications. It even creates parent directories for new files automatically.
features.robustParser: **Robust Parser**: Intelligently ignores conversational artifacts, malformed headers, and other junk that LLMs sometimes include in diff code blocks.

fuzzyLevels.title: Fuzzy Matching Levels
fuzzyLevels.intro: Mend operates on a simple but powerful principle: trust the content, not the coordinates. The search happens in stages:
fuzzyLevels.level0: **Level 0 (Strict)**: An exact, line-by-line match. The fastest and most precise when available.
fuzzyLevels.level1: **Level 1 (Whitespace Insensitive)**: Ignores leading/trailing whitespace and empty lines. Handles minor formatting differences.
fuzzyLevels.level2: **Level 2 (Anchor-Point Heuristic)**: Uses the first and last lines of a change block as anchors to find the location, even if content in between has been modified. Scores matches for similarity.
fuzzyLevels.explanation: This multi-level approach means Mend can handle everything from pristine patches to heavily mangled LLM output, falling back gracefully through each level until it finds a match.

architecture.title: Code Architecture
architecture.intro: The project is organized into focused modules:
architecture.parser: **parser.rs**: Parses unified diff format, handling headers, hunks, and extracting file metadata. Robust against malformed input.
architecture.diff: **diff.rs**: Defines the core data structures for representing diffs, hunks, and line changes.
architecture.patcher: **patcher.rs**: The heart of Mend—implements the fuzzy matching algorithm and applies changes to files safely.
architecture.error: **error.rs**: Comprehensive error handling with descriptive messages for debugging.

usage.title: Usage Guide
usage.intro: Mend is designed to be intuitive while providing powerful options for advanced use cases.

basicUsage.title: Basic Usage
basicUsage.intro: The most common operations are straightforward:

interactive.title: Interactive Mode
interactive.intro: When a patch hunk is ambiguous or cannot be applied, Mend prompts you for input with scored options:
interactive.explanation: Each option shows the line number and a similarity score (0.0-1.0). You can choose the correct location, skip the problematic hunk, or abort the entire operation safely.

opinion.title: Personal Opinion
opinion.intro: Building Mend came from a real frustration with existing patch tools when working with AI-generated code changes.
opinion.llmProblem: LLMs are incredibly useful for generating code changes, but they often produce diffs with incorrect line numbers, slightly modified context, or extra conversational text. Standard patch tools simply fail in these situations, leaving you to manually apply changes—defeating the purpose of automation.
opinion.rustChoice: I chose Rust for this project because reliability and performance are critical. When you're applying patches to your codebase, you need absolute confidence that the tool won't corrupt your files. Rust's type system and memory safety guarantees made this much easier to achieve.
opinion.fuzzyAlgorithm: The anchor-point heuristic in Level 2 matching was the key innovation. By using the first and last lines as anchors and scoring the content in between, Mend can find matches even when LLMs have made minor modifications to the context lines—something that breaks every other patch tool I've tried.
opinion.future: I use Mend daily in my workflow, and I continue to improve it based on real-world edge cases. The goal is to make it the go-to tool for anyone working with AI-assisted coding.

whatIsThis.title: What is this?
whatIsThis.p1: BlockTrack is a full-stack web application that provides a real-time leaderboard of cryptocurrency tokens sorted by market capitalization. It's designed for crypto enthusiasts who want to track the market and manage their favorite tokens.
whatIsThis.p2: Built with a modern tech stack and following Clean Architecture principles, BlockTrack demonstrates enterprise-level patterns in a personal project context. Users can authenticate, save favorites, explore detailed token metrics, and visualize historical price data.

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.intro: BlockTrack is architected as a monorepo with separate frontend and backend applications, communicating via GraphQL. The project prioritizes clean code, separation of concerns, and a premium user experience.
overview.architectureAlt: Architecture diagram showing frontend-backend communication via GraphQL

features.title: Core Features
features.leaderboard: **Real-Time Leaderboard**: View crypto tokens sortable by market cap, price, and percentage changes (1h, 24h, 7d, 30d, 1y).
features.search: **Search & Filter**: Quickly find tokens by name or symbol with instant results.
features.favorites: **Favorite Tokens**: Authenticated users can save favorites and access them on a dedicated page.
features.details: **Token Details**: Deep-dive into any token with price statistics, supply info, and interactive historical charts.
features.auth: **User Authentication**: Secure registration, login, profile management, and account deletion.
features.responsive: **Responsive Design**: Fully responsive UI adapting to all screen sizes.
features.theme: **Dark/Light Mode**: Toggle between themes for comfortable viewing.

techStack.title: Technology Stack
techStack.react: **React 19** with Vite for blazing-fast development and HMR
techStack.vite: **Vite** as the build tool for optimal developer experience
techStack.apollo: **Apollo Client** for GraphQL state management and caching
techStack.graphql: **GraphQL** with Apollo Server for flexible API queries
techStack.prisma: **Prisma** ORM with SQLite for type-safe database access

architecture.title: Architecture Deep Dive
architecture.intro: BlockTrack follows Uncle Bob's Clean Architecture to promote separation of concerns, testability, and maintainability.

cleanArch.title: Clean Architecture Layers
cleanArch.intro: Each layer has a specific responsibility and depends only on inner layers:
cleanArch.domain: **Domain Layer**: Core business logic, entities, and repository interfaces. Completely framework-independent.
cleanArch.useCases: **Use Cases Layer**: Application-specific business rules. Orchestrates data flow between domain and external layers.
cleanArch.adapters: **Interface Adapters**: Converts data formats. Includes GraphQL resolvers, repository implementations, and presenters.
cleanArch.frameworks: **Frameworks & Drivers**: External dependencies like NestJS, Prisma, React, and Apollo.

api.title: GraphQL API
api.intro: The backend exposes a comprehensive GraphQL API. You can explore it via the GraphQL Playground at /graphql when the server is running.

opinion.title: Personal Opinion
opinion.intro: BlockTrack was an ambitious project that let me explore enterprise-level architecture patterns in a full-stack context.
opinion.cleanArchChallenge: Implementing Clean Architecture properly was the biggest challenge. It's easy to understand the theory, but applying it consistently across both frontend and backend requires discipline. The payoff is a codebase that's genuinely easy to test and extend.
opinion.graphqlBenefits: Choosing GraphQL over REST was a great decision. The flexibility to request exactly the data you need, combined with Apollo's caching, makes the frontend much more efficient. The schema also serves as living documentation.
opinion.realTimeData: Working with real-time cryptocurrency data from CoinGecko taught me a lot about caching strategies, rate limiting, and handling external API failures gracefully. The backend caches data intelligently to minimize API calls while keeping information fresh.
opinion.future: Future improvements include comprehensive testing, portfolio tracking features, price alerts, and potentially containerization with Docker for easier deployment.

whatIsThis.title: What is this?
whatIsThis.p1: Investotron 2000 is a Rust-based terminal application (TUI) for cryptocurrency investment analysis. It downloads, cleans, and analyzes historical OHLCVT data from Kraken to help users make informed investment decisions.
whatIsThis.p2: The project implements a simplified Markowitz mean-variance model to optimize portfolio allocation across multiple crypto assets, offering three risk profiles: Low, Medium, and High.

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.intro: This was a group project for the R5C06 course. The application provides an end-to-end pipeline from raw data download to portfolio recommendations, all within an interactive terminal interface.
overview.tuiAlt: Terminal screenshot showing the Investotron 2000 main menu

pipeline.title: Data Pipeline
pipeline.intro: The application follows a three-phase pipeline:
pipeline.prepare: **Prepare**: Automated download of Kraken's OHLCVT archive, optional checksum verification, and extraction to data/raw.
pipeline.clean: **Clean**: Selection of USD pairs only, choosing the finest granularity available, copying to data/clean, and excluding files with too few data points.
pipeline.analyze: **Analyze**: Mean-variance portfolio optimization with risk profiles, monthly projections, and allocation recommendations.

model.title: Financial Model
model.intro: The project implements a simplified Markowitz model, a cornerstone of modern portfolio theory.

markowitz.title: Markowitz Mean-Variance Model
markowitz.intro: The model uses classical formulas for portfolio optimization:
markowitz.returns: **Daily Returns**: Computed as ln(P_t / P_t-1) using log returns for better statistical properties.
markowitz.annualized: **Annualized Metrics**: Mean and standard deviation scaled by 365 days for yearly perspective.
markowitz.portfolio: **Portfolio Statistics**: Weighted return and variance using the covariance matrix for risk assessment.
markowitz.projection: **Monthly Projection**: Compound growth formula for projecting portfolio value over time.

riskProfiles.title: Risk Profiles
riskProfiles.intro: The weight calculation blends defensive (inverse volatility) and offensive (volatility proportional) strategies:
riskProfiles.low: **Low Risk (blend=0.0)**: Pure inverse-volatility weights, targeting ~10% annual volatility. Concentrates on 2-3 stable assets.
riskProfiles.medium: **Medium Risk (blend=0.45)**: 55% defensive / 45% offensive mix, targeting ~40% volatility. Typically 6-10 positions.
riskProfiles.high: **High Risk (blend=0.70)**: 30% defensive / 70% offensive, accepting up to ~70% annual volatility for maximum expected return.

tui.title: Terminal Interface
tui.intro: The TUI provides multiple views for analyzing your portfolio:
tui.content: **Content Tab**: Detailed portfolio composition with allocation percentages for each asset.
tui.summary: **Summary Tab**: Investment amount, horizon, expected returns, and volatility metrics.
tui.graphs: **Graphs Tab**: ASCII visualization of projected portfolio value over time.
tui.advanced: **Advanced Tab**: Sample size, annualized drift, asset count, and excluded pairs information.
tui.graphAlt: Terminal graph showing projected portfolio growth over 12 months

opinion.title: Personal Opinion
opinion.intro: Building Investotron 2000 was an excellent learning experience that combined finance theory with systems programming.
opinion.rustTui: Creating a TUI in Rust was incredibly satisfying. The ecosystem has matured significantly, and libraries like ratatui make it straightforward to build responsive, visually appealing terminal applications.
opinion.mathModel: Implementing the Markowitz model from scratch deepened my understanding of portfolio theory. Translating mathematical formulas into working code—handling edge cases, numerical stability, and real-world data quirks—is very different from textbook examples.
opinion.teamwork: This was a group project, and coordinating the data pipeline, financial model, and UI required good communication. We divided responsibilities clearly: data handling, analytics engine, and interface development.
opinion.limitations: The model has known limitations: no transaction costs, no handling of missing values within series, and VaR/CVaR metrics are placeholder. These are documented and would be natural extensions for future work.

whatIsThis.title: What is this?
whatIsThis.p1: SAE Music Analysis is a comprehensive music recommendation system built from scratch as a school project. It demonstrates the full data science pipeline from raw data cleaning to multiple recommendation algorithms, including neural networks.
whatIsThis.p2: The project shows systematic performance improvements across versions, from basic text-based recommendations to sophisticated multi-modal similarity scoring using audio features, temporal characteristics, and user preferences.

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.intro: This was a major SAE (Situation d'Apprentissage et d'Évaluation) project involving multiple tracks and team collaboration. The goal was to build a complete music platform with data analysis, database design, and recommendation systems.

tracks.title: Project Tracks
tracks.t1: **Track 1 - Data Analysis**: Cleaning, validating, and merging multiple music datasets (tracks, artists, albums, genres, audio features).
tracks.t2: **Track 2 - Database**: PostgreSQL schema design with normalized tables for music domain and user preferences, running in Docker.
tracks.t3: **Track 3 - Recommendation**: Multiple recommendation algorithms including item-based, user-based, and neural network approaches.

database.title: Database Architecture
database.intro: The database was designed to support both the music catalog and user interactions, enabling various recommendation strategies.

schema.title: Schema Design
schema.track: **track**: Core music metadata including title, duration, explicit flag, listen counts, and creation date.
schema.artist: **artist**: Artist information with biography, location, activity years, and popularity metrics.
schema.album: **album**: Album details with type, track count, release date, and engagement statistics.
schema.audioFeature: **audio_feature**: Spotify-like audio features—acousticness, danceability, energy, instrumentalness, liveness, speechiness, tempo, valence.
schema.temporalFeature: **temporal_feature**: Extensive audio analysis including MFCC coefficients, spectral features, chroma, and tonnetz (200+ features per track).
schema.user: **user/preference**: User accounts with detailed listening preferences and consent tracking.
schema.features: The schema supports junction tables for many-to-many relationships (track-genre, track-artist, playlist-track) and dedicated tables for rankings and licenses.

recommenders.title: Recommendation Algorithms
recommenders.intro: We implemented multiple recommendation approaches, each with different trade-offs and use cases.

itemBased.title: Item-Based Audio Similarity
itemBased.intro: Uses audio features to find similar tracks. Supports weighted similarity combining audio features with optional random noise for diversity:

userBased.title: User-Based Collaborative Filtering
userBased.intro: Creates user preference vectors from listening history and finds similar users to recommend tracks they enjoyed. Uses cosine similarity on preference embeddings.

neuralNetwork.title: Neural Network Model
neuralNetwork.intro: An MLP (Multi-Layer Perceptron) trained to predict track listens based on audio features:
neuralNetwork.training: The model uses 80/20 train-test split with 10% validation, SmoothL1Loss for robustness to outliers, and learning rate scheduling for convergence.

dataProcessing.title: Data Processing Pipeline
dataProcessing.intro: Track 1 focused on preparing the data for analysis and database population:
dataProcessing.cleaning: **Cleaning**: Validation rules in globalrules.py, type checking, and standardization (text normalization, date formats).
dataProcessing.validation: **Validation**: CleanReport generation showing applied rules and data quality metrics.
dataProcessing.merging: **Merging**: Joining clean_tracks.csv with genres, albums, artists, and audio features into merged_tracks.csv.
dataProcessing.visualization: **Visualization**: Automated graph generation for data exploration and reporting.

opinion.title: Personal Opinion
opinion.intro: This SAE project was one of the most comprehensive data science experiences I've had in school.
opinion.dataChallenge: The data cleaning phase taught me that 80% of data science is data preparation. Handling inconsistent formats, missing values, and merging multiple sources requires careful attention to detail.
opinion.iterativeApproach: We iterated through multiple recommendation versions, each improving on the last. Starting with simple text matching, then moving to audio features, and finally to neural networks showed how incremental improvements compound.
opinion.teamCollaboration: Working as a team on interconnected tracks (data, database, recommendations) required good coordination. We maintained clear interfaces between components so each person could work independently.
opinion.learnings: The project reinforced that recommendation systems are as much about data quality as algorithm sophistication. A simple algorithm on clean, well-structured data often outperforms complex models on messy data.

whatIsThis.title: What is this?
whatIsThis.p1: This portfolio website is a personal project showcasing my work, skills, and approach to software development. It's built with modern web technologies and serves as both a presentation layer and a technical demonstration.
whatIsThis.p2: The site features full internationalization (English/French), dark/light theme support, smooth animations, and a blog-style project detail system that you're reading right now.

overview.title: Project Overview
overview.intro: Built with Next.js 16 and the App Router, this portfolio emphasizes performance, accessibility, and developer experience. Every component is carefully crafted for both aesthetics and functionality.

techStack.title: Technology Stack
techStack.nextjs: **Next.js 16**: App Router with Turbopack for fast development and optimized production builds.
techStack.react: **React 19**: Latest React features including Server Components and improved hydration.
techStack.tailwind: **Tailwind CSS v4**: Utility-first styling with the latest version's improvements.
techStack.radix: **Radix UI**: Accessible, unstyled primitives for dropdown menus, switches, and tabs.
techStack.gsap: **GSAP**: Professional-grade animations with ScrollTrigger for scroll-based effects.
techStack.nextThemes: **next-themes**: Seamless dark/light mode with system preference detection.

i18n.title: Internationalization
i18n.intro: The site supports English and French with locale-aware routing (/en/..., /fr/...). Translations are type-safe and organized by feature:

theming.title: Theme System
theming.intro: Dark and light themes are implemented with next-themes, respecting system preferences by default. CSS variables ensure consistent theming across all components, and the toggle provides instant, flicker-free switching.

animations.title: Animations
animations.intro: GSAP powers smooth, performant animations throughout the site. ScrollTrigger enables elements to animate as they enter the viewport:

structure.title: Project Structure
structure.intro: The codebase follows Next.js conventions with a clear separation of concerns:

opinion.title: Personal Opinion
opinion.intro: Building my own portfolio has been an ongoing journey of refinement and learning.
opinion.nextjsExperience: Next.js 16 with the App Router represents the future of React development. Server Components, streaming, and Turbopack make development incredibly fast while producing optimized production builds.
opinion.i18nChallenge: Implementing i18n properly was more complex than expected. Beyond translation strings, you need to handle locale detection, routing, SEO metadata, and ensuring the correct language loads on first render without flicker.
opinion.designPhilosophy: I wanted a design that's professional but not generic. The combination of subtle gradients, glass-morphism effects, and thoughtful animations creates a distinctive feel while remaining accessible and performant.
opinion.continuousImprovement: This portfolio is never 'done.' I continuously add new projects, refine the design, and experiment with new techniques. It's both a showcase and a learning playground.

projectOne.title: My QOL Scripts Minecraft Mod

It provides a high-performance JavaScript engine powered by GraalJS, enabling players to create complex scripts that enhance their gameplay through a rich set of APIs including event handling, custom commands, keybinds, configuration management, and runtime Java method hooking.

projectTwo.title: Mend

Authenticated users can select and store their favorite tokens, explore detailed token information including historical price charts, and manage their user profile.
